claim: Population neural activity more accurately decodes locomotion than any single neuron in C. elegans.
source: We report that population activity more accurately decodes locomotion than any single neuron.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 comparing population decoder performance to best single neuron performance.

claim: Relevant locomotory signals are distributed across neurons with diverse tunings to locomotion in C. elegans.
source: Relevant signals are distributed across neurons with diverse tunings to locomotion.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 1 and Figure 5 showing neurons with varied tuning curves to velocity and curvature.

claim: Two largely distinct subpopulations of neurons are informative for decoding velocity and curvature in C. elegans.
source: Two largely distinct subpopulations are informative for decoding velocity and curvature, and different neurons' activities contribute features relevant for different aspects of a behavior or different instances of a behavioral motif.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 6 showing minimal overlap between neurons used for velocity versus curvature decoding.

claim: Different neurons' activities contribute features relevant for different aspects of a behavior or different instances of a behavioral motif in C. elegans.
source: Two largely distinct subpopulations are informative for decoding velocity and curvature, and different neurons' activities contribute features relevant for different aspects of a behavior or different instances of a behavioral motif.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and illustrated in Figure 5c,d showing different neurons contributing to different instances of reversals or turns.

claim: AVAL and AVAR activity exhibits expected transients during backward locomotion in moving C. elegans.
source: To validate our measurements, we labeled neurons AVAL and AVAR and found that their activity exhibited expected transients during backward locomotion.
evidence: This validation is stated in the abstract and shown in Figure 2b with calcium activity traces aligned to velocity.

claim: Immobilization alters the correlation structure of neural activity in C. elegans.
source: Immobilization alters the correlation structure of neural activity and its dynamics.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 7e,f showing changes in pairwise neural correlations between moving and immobile states.

claim: Some neurons positively correlated with AVA during movement become negatively correlated during immobilization and vice versa.
source: Some neurons positively correlated with AVA during movement become negatively correlated during immobilization and vice versa.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and shown in Figure 8 with specific examples of neurons changing correlation sign with AVA.

claim: Immobilization alters the dynamics of neural activity in C. elegans.
source: Immobilization alters the correlation structure of neural activity and its dynamics.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated in Figure 7c,d showing different neural state space trajectories during movement versus immobilization.

claim: Place cells have been revealed through single-unit recordings in neuroscience.
source: Such efforts have successfully revealed place cells (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971) and head direction cells (Taube et al., 1990; Hafting et al., 2005), for example.
evidence: This is a citation to prior work establishing the existence of place cells.

claim: Head direction cells have been revealed through single-unit recordings in neuroscience.
source: Such efforts have successfully revealed place cells (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971) and head direction cells (Taube et al., 1990; Hafting et al., 2005), for example.
evidence: This is a citation to prior work establishing the existence of head direction cells.

claim: Population recordings from the central complex in Drosophila reveal that the animal's heading is represented in the population by a bump of neural activity in a ring attractor network.
source: For example, population recordings from the central complex in Drosophila reveal that the animal's heading is represented in the population by a bump of neural activity in a ring attractor network (Kim et al., 2017; Green et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a citation to prior work on heading representation in Drosophila.

claim: Neural signals that correlate with rodent facial expression and body motion were recently reported in visual cortex.
source: For example, neural signals that correlate with rodent facial expression and body motion were recently reported in sensory areas such as visual cortex (Stringer et al., 2019) and in executive decision making areas of dorsal cortex (Musall et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a citation to recent work on locomotory signals in rodent visual cortex.

claim: Neural signals that correlate with rodent facial expression and body motion were recently reported in executive decision making areas of dorsal cortex.
source: For example, neural signals that correlate with rodent facial expression and body motion were recently reported in sensory areas such as visual cortex (Stringer et al., 2019) and in executive decision making areas of dorsal cortex (Musall et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a citation to recent work on locomotory signals in rodent dorsal cortex.

claim: The known locomotory circuitry in C. elegans includes pre-motor neurons and interneurons such as AVA, AVE, AVB, AIB, AIZ, RIM, RIA, RIV, RIB, and PVC.
source: The known locomotory circuitry in C. elegans focuses on a collection of pre-motor neurons and interneurons, including AVA, AVE, AVB, AIB, AIZ, RIM, RIA, RIV, RIB, and PVC that have many connections amongst themselves and send signals to downstream motor neurons involved in locomotion such as the A- or B-type or SMD motor neurons (White et al., 1976; Chalfie et al., 1985; Zheng et al., 1999; Gray et al., 2005; Gordus et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work characterizing the locomotory circuitry.

claim: AVA, AIB, and RIM are part of a backward locomotory circuit in C. elegans.
source: For example, AVA, AIB, and RIM are part of a backward locomotory circuit (Zheng et al., 1999; Pirri et al., 2009; Gordus et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work on backward locomotion circuitry.

claim: AVB and PVC are part of a forward locomotion circuit in C. elegans.
source: AVB and PVC are part of a forward locomotion circuit (Gray et al., 2005; Chalfie et al., 1985; Zheng et al., 1999; Li et al., 2011; Roberts et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2018);
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work on forward locomotion circuitry.

claim: RIV, RIB, and RIA are related to turns in C. elegans.
source: and RIV, RIB, and RIA are related to turns (Gray et al., 2005; Li et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2020; Hendricks et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work on turning behavior.

claim: Much of what we know about locomotory neurons in C. elegans comes from recordings or manipulations of either single neurons at a time, or a selection of neurons simultaneously using sparse promoters.
source: Much of what we know about these neurons comes from recordings or manipulations of either single neurons at a time, or a selection of neurons simultaneously using sparse promoters (Gray et al., 2005; Guo et al., 2009; Ben Arous et al., 2010; Kawano et al., 2011; Piggott et al., 2011; Gao et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work using single or sparse neuron recordings.

claim: It has only recently become possible to record from large populations of neurons first in immobile and then moving C. elegans.
source: Only recently has it been possible to record from large populations of neurons first in immobile (Schrödel et al., 2013; Prevedel et al., 2014; Kato et al., 2015) and then moving animals (Nguyen et al., 2016; Venkatachalam et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citations to recent technological advances in population recording.

claim: There has not yet been a systematic exploration of the types and distribution of locomotor related signals present in the neural population during movement and their tunings in C. elegans.
source: There has not yet been a systematic exploration of the types and distribution of locomotor related signals present in the neural population during movement and their tunings.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: Results from recordings in immobile C. elegans suggest that population neural state space trajectories in a low dimensional space may encode global motor commands.
source: Interestingly, results from recordings in immobile animals suggest that population neural state space trajectories in a low dimensional space may encode global motor commands (Kato et al., 2015), but this has yet to be explored in moving animals.
evidence: This is a citation to prior work on neural state space in immobilized animals.

claim: It is not known how locomotory related information contained at the population level compares to that contained at the level of single neurons in C. elegans.
source: it is not known how locomotory related information contained at the population level compares to that contained at the level of single neurons.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: It is not known for C. elegans how neural population dynamics during immobile fictive locomotion compare to population dynamics during actual movement.
source: it is not known for C. elegans how neural population dynamics during immobile fictive locomotion compare to population dynamics during actual movement.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: Calcium activity was simultaneously recorded from 134 neurons during locomotion in recording AML310_A.
source: Calcium activity of 134 neurons is simultaneously recorded during locomotion.
evidence: This is stated in the figure caption for Figure 1a and shown in the heatmap.

claim: Multiple neurons have calcium activity significantly tuned to velocity in C. elegans during movement.
source: We found multiple neurons with calcium activity significantly tuned to either velocity or curvature (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 1d and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Multiple neurons have calcium activity significantly tuned to curvature in C. elegans during movement.
source: We found multiple neurons with calcium activity significantly tuned to either velocity or curvature (Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and demonstrated in Figure 1e and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Some neurons are more active during forward locomotion while others are more active during backward locomotion in C. elegans.
source: Some neurons were more active during forward locomotion while others were more active during backward locomotion (Figure 1d and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1d with examples of neurons with positive and negative correlations to velocity.

claim: Some neurons are active during dorsal bends and others during ventral bends in C. elegans.
source: Similarly some neurons were active during dorsal bends and others during ventral bends (Figure 1e and Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1e with examples of neurons tuned to curvature.

claim: In some cases, the derivative of neural activity is significantly correlated with features of locomotion in C. elegans.
source: In some cases, the derivative of the activity was also significantly correlated with features of locomotion.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 1d,e with examples of dF/dt tuning curves.

claim: AVAL and AVAR are a bilaterally symmetric pair of neurons with gap junctions between them in C. elegans.
source: These two neurons, called AVA, are a bilaterally symmetric pair with gap junctions between them that have been shown to exhibit large calcium transients that begin with the onset of backward locomotion, peak around the end of backward locomotion during the onset of forward locomotion, and then slowly decay (Ben Arous et al., 2010; Kawano et al., 2011; Faumont et al., 2011; Shipley et al., 2014; Gordus et al., 2015; Kato et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work characterizing AVA neurons.

claim: AVA neurons exhibit large calcium transients that begin with the onset of backward locomotion, peak around the end of backward locomotion during the onset of forward locomotion, and then slowly decay.
source: These two neurons, called AVA, are a bilaterally symmetric pair with gap junctions between them that have been shown to exhibit large calcium transients that begin with the onset of backward locomotion, peak around the end of backward locomotion during the onset of forward locomotion, and then slowly decay (Ben Arous et al., 2010; Kawano et al., 2011; Faumont et al., 2011; Shipley et al., 2014; Gordus et al., 2015; Kato et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work and confirmed by data in Figure 2b.

claim: The activities of AVAL and AVAR are similar to one another in moving C. elegans.
source: Here we resolve both AVAL and AVAR and find that their activities are similar to one another, and they both exhibit the expected transients timed to backward locomotion, Figure 2b.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2b with activity traces of both neurons.

claim: Signal-to-noise in AVAR is higher than AVAL in recording AML310_A because AVAR lies closer to the imaging objective lens.
source: Signal-to-noise in AVAR is higher than AVAL because in this recording AVAR lies closer to the imaging objective lens, while AVAL is on the opposite side of the head and therefore must be imaged through the rest of the brain.
evidence: This is stated in the text as an explanation for differences in signal quality between the two neurons.

claim: AVA's activity alone is insufficient to robustly decode velocity in C. elegans.
source: AVA's activity is related to the animal's velocity, but its activity alone is insufficient to robustly decode velocity.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 2c showing AVA is informative during backward but not forward locomotion.

claim: AVA is informative during backward locomotion, but contains little information about velocity during forward locomotion in C. elegans.
source: For example, AVA is informative during backward locomotion, but contains little information about velocity during forward locomotion, Figure 2c.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 2c with AVA's tuning curve.

claim: Linear combinations of activity from the neural population in primate motor cortex provides more information about the direction of a monkey's arm motion during a reach task than a single neuron.
source: In primate motor cortex, for example, linear combinations of activity from the neural population provides more information about the direction of a monkey's arm motion during a reach task than a single neuron (Georgopoulos et al., 1986).
evidence: This is a citation to prior work on population coding in primate motor cortex.

claim: Multiple neurons in C. elegans have activity related to the animal's velocity or curvature.
source: In C. elegans, recordings from single or sparse sets of neurons show that multiple neurons have activity related to the animal's velocity or curvature (Ben Arous et al., 2010; Kocabas et al., 2012; Kawano et al., 2011; Piggott et al., 2011; Gordus et al., 2015; Kato et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work on individual neurons related to locomotion.

claim: The population model significantly outperformed the best single neuron at decoding velocity in held-out test data across 11 moving animals (p < 0.05 two-sided Wilcoxon rank test).
source: The population significantly outperformed the best single neuron at decoding the held-out portions of the recordings for both velocity and curvature (p < 0.05 two-sided Wilcoxon rank test).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3e with statistical comparison.

claim: The population model significantly outperformed the best single neuron at decoding curvature in held-out test data across 11 moving animals (p < 0.05 two-sided Wilcoxon rank test).
source: The population significantly outperformed the best single neuron at decoding the held-out portions of the recordings for both velocity and curvature (p < 0.05 two-sided Wilcoxon rank test).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3f with statistical comparison.

claim: Performance of the decoder across recordings correlated with the maximal Fano factor across neurons of the raw time-varying GCaMP fluorescence intensity.
source: Performance across recordings correlated with one metric of the signal in our recordings, the maximal Fano factor across neurons of the raw time-varying GCaMP fluorescence intensity,
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Variability in decoder performance may be due in part to variability in the amount of neural signal in the recordings.
source: This suggests that variability in performance may be due in part to variability in the amount of neural signal in our recordings.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the correlation between Fano factor and performance.

claim: In recording AML32_A, the best single neuron captures velocity dynamics for negative velocities, but saturates at positive velocities.
source: Recording AML32_A shows a striking example: the best single neuron captures velocity dynamics for negative velocities, but saturates at positive velocities.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4.

claim: The population decoder in recording AML32_A captures velocity dynamics during both forward and backward locomotion during the held-out test set.
source: The population decoder, by contrast, captures velocity dynamics during both forward and backward locomotion during the held-out test set, and covers a larger fraction of the held-out velocity range, see Figure 4.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4.

claim: Motion artifacts should affect both GCaMP and RFP fluorophores similarly.
source: We assume that these artifacts are common to both GCaMP and RFP fluorescence, up to a scale factor, because both experience the same motion.
evidence: This is stated as an assumption underlying the motion correction method.

claim: The decoder's performance relies on neural signals rather than primarily on motion artifact.
source: suggesting that the decoder's performance relies on neural signals.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the comparison between GCaMP and GFP control recordings.

claim: A simple linear combination of neurons performs better at decoding velocity or curvature than the best single neuron in C. elegans.
source: Taken together, we find that a simple linear combination of neurons performs better at decoding velocity or curvature than the best single neuron, and that the population decoder is not primarily relying on motion artifact.
evidence: This is stated as a summary conclusion based on the data presented.

claim: The population decoder is not primarily relying on motion artifact.
source: Taken together, we find that a simple linear combination of neurons performs better at decoding velocity or curvature than the best single neuron, and that the population decoder is not primarily relying on motion artifact.
evidence: This is stated as a summary conclusion based on the GFP control experiments.

claim: In the exemplar recording AML310_A, the distribution of weights for both velocity and curvature are well-approximated by a Gaussian distribution centered at zero.
source: In the exemplar recording from Figure 1, the distribution of weights for both velocity and curvature are indeed both well-approximated by a Gaussian distribution centered at zero.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5a,b.

claim: The decoder does not need to deviate significantly from the prior in order to perform well.
source: This suggests that the decoder does not need to deviate significantly from the prior in order to perform well.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the weight distributions.

claim: The decoder relies roughly equally on neurons that are positively and negatively tuned to velocity.
source: In particular, although changing the sign of any weight would not incur a regularization penalty, the decoder relies roughly equally on neurons that are positively and negatively tuned to velocity, and similarly for curvature.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5a,b.

claim: The decoder relies roughly equally on neurons that are positively and negatively tuned to curvature.
source: In particular, although changing the sign of any weight would not incur a regularization penalty, the decoder relies roughly equally on neurons that are positively and negatively tuned to velocity, and similarly for curvature.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5a,b.

claim: Some highly weighted neurons had activity traces that appeared visually similar to the animal's locomotory trace for the duration of the recording.
source: Some highly weighted neurons had activity traces that appeared visually similar to the animal's locomotory trace for the duration of the recording (e.g.#80 for curvature)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5d.

claim: Some highly weighted neurons had activity that might plausibly be noisy copies of each other.
source: and other neurons had activity that might plausibly be noisy copies of each other (e.g. #12 and #60 for velocity).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Some highly weighted neurons had activity traces that were distinct or only matched specific features of the locomotory behavior.
source: But other highly weighted neurons had activity traces that were distinct or only matched specific features of the locomotory behavior.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5c,d with specific examples.

claim: Neuron SMDD exhibits peaks during dorsal but not ventral head bends in C. elegans.
source: This is consistent with prior reports of neurons such as SMDD that are known to exhibit peaks during dorsal but not ventral head bends (Hendricks et al., 2012; Shen et al., 2016; Kaplan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work on SMDD neuron activity.

claim: In the exemplar recording, some neurons have activity matched to only specific instances of a behavior motif.
source: In the recording shown, we also find some neurons that have activity matched to only specific instances of a behavior motif.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5d with specific examples.

claim: The decoder is not primarily averaging over duplicate signals.
source: From this inspection of highly weighted neurons, we conclude that in at least some recordings the decoder is not primarily averaging over duplicate signals.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on inspection of highly weighted neurons in Figure 5.

claim: The decoder sums together different types of neural signals, including those that capture only a certain feature of a behavior or that seemingly capture only certain instance of the same behavior motif.
source: Instead the decoder sums together different types of neural signals, including those that capture only a certain feature of a behavior (e.g. dorsal turns or ventral turns, but not both) or that seemingly capture only certain instance of the same behavior motif (some reversals but not others).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on inspection of highly weighted neurons in Figure 5.

claim: For the exemplar recording AML310_A, 90% of the model's performance was achieved when including only 13 neurons for velocity.
source: For the exemplar recording AML310_A, 90% of the model's performance was achieved when including only 13 neurons for velocity, and only four neurons for curvature.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6a.

claim: For the exemplar recording AML310_A, 90% of the model's performance was achieved when including only four neurons for curvature.
source: For the exemplar recording AML310_A, 90% of the model's performance was achieved when including only 13 neurons for velocity, and only four neurons for curvature.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6a.

claim: Across all recordings, there was a median of 27 neurons needed to achieve 90% of full model performance for velocity.
source: Across all recordings, we saw large variability in the number of important neurons N90 (Figure 6b,c and Table 1) with a median of 27 neurons for velocity and 31 for curvature.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6b and Table 1.

claim: Across all recordings, there was a median of 31 neurons needed to achieve 90% of full model performance for curvature.
source: Across all recordings, we saw large variability in the number of important neurons N90 (Figure 6b,c and Table 1) with a median of 27 neurons for velocity and 31 for curvature.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 6b and Table 1.

claim: The recordings contained a median total of 121 neurons.
source: By comparison, our recordings contained a median total of 121 neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Table 1.

claim: On average, the decoder relies on roughly a quarter of the neurons in a recording to achieve the majority of its decoding performance.
source: On average, the decoder relies on roughly a quarter of the neurons in a recording to achieve the majority of its decoding performance.
evidence: This is stated as a summary based on the N90 values compared to total neuron counts.

claim: Most neurons that have been well characterized in the literature have been ascribed roles to either velocity or curvature but not both.
source: Most neurons that have been well characterized in the literature, such as AVE and SMD, have been ascribed roles to either velocity or curvature but not both.
evidence: This is stated based on knowledge from the literature.

claim: RIB may be an exception and has recently been proposed to be involved in both reversals and turns in C. elegans.
source: RIB may be exception, and has recently been proposed to be involved in both reversals and turns (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with citation to recent work on RIB.

claim: Largely distinct sub-populations of neurons in the brain contain the majority of information important for decoding velocity and curvature.
source: Taken together, this suggests that largely distinct sub-populations of neurons in the brain contain the majority of information important for decoding velocity and curvature.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the small overlap between velocity and curvature N90 populations.

claim: Recordings of brain-wide calcium activity of immobilized C. elegans provided evidence to suggest that the population may be involved in representing locomotion or motor commands.
source: Recordings of brain-wide calcium activity of immobilized C. elegans provided evidence to suggest that the population may be involved in representing locomotion or motor commands (Kato et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with citation to prior work on immobilized recordings.

claim: Motor commands may be represented as neural trajectories through a low-dimensional state space defined by principal components determined by the correlation structure of population neural activity.
source: Specifically these motor commands may be represented as neural trajectories through a low-dimensional state space defined by principal components determined by the correlation structure of population neural activity in the recording.
evidence: This is stated with reference to prior work on neural state space in immobilized animals.

claim: Neuron RIM exhibited seemingly slower dynamics in immobilized population recordings than in sparse recordings during movement.
source: For example, neuron RIM exhibited seemingly slower dynamics in immobilized population recordings than in sparse recordings during movement.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from prior work comparing immobilized and moving recordings.

claim: Immobilization changed the correlation structure of neural activity in C. elegans.
source: Immobilization changed the correlation structure of neural activity.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7e.

claim: Clusters of neurons that had been correlated with one another during movement were no longer correlated during immobilization.
source: Clusters of neurons that had been correlated with one another during movement were no longer correlated during immobilization (see Figure 7e, top row, blocks of contiguous yellow on the diagonal during movement that are absent or disrupted during immobilization ).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7e.

claim: Many neurons that had been only weakly positively correlated or had negative correlations during movement became strongly positively correlated with one another during immobilization.
source: Notably, many neurons that had been only weakly positively correlated or had negative correlations during movement became strongly positively correlated with one another during immobilization forming a large block (Figure 7e, bottom, large contiguous yellow square that appears on the lower right along the diagonal during immobilization).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7e.

claim: Immobilization alters the correlation structure more than would occur by chance in a moving worm.
source: This suggests that immobilization alters the correlation structure more than would occur by chance in a moving worm.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the statistical comparison in Figure 7f.

claim: Neural state space trajectories during immobilization were more structured and stereotyped than during movement.
source: Neural state space trajectories during immobilization were more structured and stereotyped than during movement and exhibited similarities to previous reports, see Figure 7c,d.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7c,d.

claim: The emergence of structured neural state-space dynamics during immobilization is consistent with the significant change to the correlation structure observed in neural activity.
source: The emergence of structured neural state-space dynamics during immobilization is consistent with the significant change to the correlation structure observed in neural activity.
evidence: This is stated as an inference connecting the changes in correlation structure to changes in dynamics.

claim: Immobilization alters the correlation structure and dynamics of neural activity and may have implications for the interpretation of immobile neural dynamics.
source: Taken together, these measurements suggest that immobilization alters the correlation structure and dynamics of neural activity and may have implications for the interpretation of immobile neural dynamics.
evidence: This is stated as a summary conclusion based on the data presented.

claim: During movement AVA exhibited a sharp rise in response to most instances of the animal's backward locomotion.
source: During movement AVA exhibited a sharp rise in response to most instances of the animal's backward locomotion, as expected (Figure 7b).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7b.

claim: During immobilization, AVA exhibited slow cycles of activity captured in one of the first three PCs.
source: During immobilization, AVA exhibited slow cycles of activity captured in one of the first three PCs.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 7b,c.

claim: Immobilization induced many neurons to change the sign of their correlations with AVA.
source: Interestingly, immobilization induced many neurons to change the sign of their correlations with AVA.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 8.

claim: Some neurons that had negative correlation coefficients with respect to AVA during movement had positive correlation coefficients during immobilization.
source: For example, some neurons, such as #43 and #44, that had negative correlation coefficients with respect to AVA during movement but had positive correlation coefficients during immobilization (Fig Figure 8a,b,d).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 8.

claim: Some neurons that had positive correlation coefficients with respect to AVA during movement had negative correlation coefficients with respect to AVA during immobilization.
source: Similarly, some neurons, such as #23 and #33 that had positive correlation coefficients with respect to AVA during movement, had negative correlation coefficients with respect to AVA during immobilization.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 8.

claim: On average, neurons in recording AML310_E become significantly more positively correlated to AVA upon immobilization than during movement (p = 0.019 Wilcoxon ranked test).
source: On average, neurons in this recording become significantly more positively correlated to AVA upon immobilization than during movement (p = 0.019 Wilcoxon ranked test), Figure 8c.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 8c with statistical comparison.

claim: Immobilization significantly alters the correlation structure of neural activity in C. elegans.
source: Taken together, our measurements show that immobilization significantly alters the correlation structure of neural activity.
evidence: This is stated as a summary conclusion based on the data presented.

claim: Immobilization causes neurons to change their correlation with AVA from negatively correlated to positively correlated, or vice versa.
source: Immobilization also causes neurons to change their correlation with known well-characterized neurons, like AVA, from negatively correlated to positively correlated, or vice versa.
evidence: This is stated as a summary conclusion based on the data in Figure 8.

claim: A linear decoder can predict the animal's current velocity and body curvature from neural signals in the population.
source: Our measurements show that a linear decoder can predict the animal's current velocity and body curvature from neural signals in the population.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the main finding.

claim: A linear combination of activity from different neurons is one plausible mechanism that the brain may employ to represent behavior.
source: This suggests that a linear combination of activity from different neurons is one plausible mechanism that the brain may employ to represent behavior.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the decoder's success.

claim: The measurements do not distinguish between neural signals that drive locomotion and neural signals that monitor locomotion generated elsewhere.
source: And in all cases, the measurements here do not distinguish between neural signals that drive locomotion, such as motor commands; and neural signals that monitor locomotion generated elsewhere, such as proprioceptive feedback (Wen et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the current study.

claim: The decoder likely uses a mix of both motor command signals and proprioceptive feedback signals.
source: The decoder likely uses a mix of both.
evidence: This is stated as an inference about the nature of signals used by the decoder.

claim: Future perturbation studies are needed to distinguish population-level signals that drive locomotion from those that monitor locomotion.
source: Future perturbation studies are needed to distinguish population-level signals that drive locomotion from those that monitor locomotion.
evidence: This is stated as a suggestion for future work.

claim: Even very non-linear neural systems can encode information linearly.
source: It has been observed that even very non-linear neural systems can encode information linearly.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge from neuroscience.

claim: The vertebrate retina has many highly non-linear connections but a linear decoder performs indistinguishably from an artificial neural network at decoding visual signals from populations of retinal ganglion cells.
source: For example, the vertebrate retina has many highly non-linear connections but a linear decoder performs indistinguishably from an (nonlinear) artificial neural network at decoding visual signals from populations of retinal ganglion cells (Warland et al., 1997).
evidence: This is a citation to prior work on linear decoding in the retina.

claim: C. elegans may be another example of a non-linear system that represents information linearly.
source: C. elegans may be another example, like the retina, of a non-linear system that represents information linearly.
evidence: This is stated as speculation based on the findings.

claim: The C. elegans nervous system contains known instances of connections that appear linear over a physiologically relevant range of activities.
source: The C. elegans nervous system, however, also contains known instances of connections that appear linear over a physiologically relevant range of activities (Liu et al., 2009; Lindsay et al., 2011; Narayan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work on linear connections in C. elegans.

claim: It is possible that the linear representation of behavior in C. elegans reflects linear circuitry in the brain.
source: So, it is also possible that the linear representation of behavior in C. elegans reflects linear circuitry in the brain.
evidence: This is stated as speculation about the interpretation of the findings.

claim: It is possible that a different non-linear model would perform better than the linear model tested.
